item.title: Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes with reduced efficiency roll-off via accelerated exciton utilization
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02029-4 Deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes leveraging phosphor-assisted TADF-sensitized fluorescence enable accelerated exciton dynamics, resulting in devices with an external quantum efficiency of 35.9% and an LT80 lifetime of 632 h.

item.title: Phase control of interfering stimulated Raman pathways in the XUV regime
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02024-9 Researchers modulate population transfer from the helium ground state to a metastable state by controlling the relative phase between two interfering stimulated Raman pathways through the continuum, demonstrating phase-coherent control in the extreme ultraviolet.

item.title: Engineering the unknown: building vacuum and cryogenic systems for the quantum frontier
item.description: Qubit decoherence remains the primary barrier to many practical quantum devices. item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers.

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies.

item.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. This has resulted in two technologies that are widespread today: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is commonplace in hospitals, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is used to determine the structures of proteins and

item.title: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
item.description: Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
item.description: Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

item.title: Nonlinear circular dichroism reveals the local Berry curvature
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02025-8 The nonlinear high harmonic circular dichroism for crystals with broken time-reversal symmetry is found to be directly proportional to the local Berry curvature, and it can be directly probed via ultrafast all-optical measurements.

item.title: From spin wave to superconducting circuit: A one-way street for quantum information
item.description: Quantum information systems could one day shape everyday life through faster computing, sharper sensing and more secure communication. A new result from the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U. of I.) marks an important step toward enabling magnetic spins—a quantum property of matter that can be used to store and manipulate information—to play a role in the future of quantum information processing.

item.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
item.description: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power memories and logic circuits. IBM executive warns of risk of quantum computing hacks
item.description: Organizations are unprepared for the risks posed by quantum computing, IBM's Europe and Africa vice president Alessandro Curioni told AFP Wednesday, referring to the high-speed technology that could crack security encryptions and enable large-scale cyberattacks.

item.title: 'Carpet' growth method yields long-sought 2D quantum material
item.description: For decades, physicists have sought a practical two-dimensional topological insulator: an ultrathin material whose interior blocks electricity but whose edges conduct it. In ordinary wires, electrons constantly bounce off imperfections, losing energy. But along the edges of a 2D topological insulator, electrons with opposite spins travel in opposite directions, like cars in one-way lanes, so they rarely scatter and lose energy.
